evidence_quotes.quote: examine the intersection of groundwater level changes (availability), socioeconomic and regulatory factors (access), and nitrate and arsenic contamination (quality) across 1881 groundwater-supplied drinking water service areas in Arizona.

We hypothesize that groundwater availability, measured by changes in groundwater levels, is shaped by access factors and water quality, with greater declines expected in areas with unregulated water supplies, weaker regulatory oversight, vulnerable aquifers, and disadvantaged communities.

The 1980 Groundwater Management Act (GMA) established Active Management Areas (AMAs) to regulate groundwater in regions with significant depletion. AMAs cover over 80% of Arizona’s population and are governed by strict regulations to balance annual groundwater withdrawals with natural or artificial recharge.

Water systems in these areas were categorized as either community water systems (CWS), regulated under the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA), or domestic well areas (DWAs), which primarily rely on unregulated private domestic wells [3,5,10]. Of the 1881 mapped service areas, 55.3% were designated as CWS and 44.7% were designated as DWAs.

Groundwater availability trends in subbasins containing drinking water sources were evaluated using rates of water level change as proxies for available quantities. Groundwater level changes over 20-year (2001–2020) and 10-year (2011–2020) periods were calculated using ADWR index well data.
Water quality variables were analyzed as continuous measures of contaminant concentrations (ValueImp1) and binary indicators for detection (Detect) and regulatory exceedance (MCLExceeded).

criterion_notes.c1: No. Although the title and conceptual 'trivalent framework' use the word 'access', the paper defines 'access' as static service-area predictor attributes (water supply type CWS vs DWA, GMA and SDWA regulatory designations, aquifer type, and Census socioeconomic/housing demographics) across 1,881 already-delineated drinking water service areas. It studies hydrogeological subbasin groundwater-table depletion/recharge and source groundwater arsenic/nitrate contamination rather than household or community water service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — the study includes regulatory and governance classifications in its statistical models, specifically Arizona 1980 Groundwater Management Act (GMA) designations (Active Management Areas/Irrigation Non-Expansion Areas vs Non-Designated Areas), Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) regulatory primacy (Tribal vs State oversight), and SDWA-regulated Community Water Systems (CWS) vs unregulated exempt Domestic Well Areas (DWAs). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification: NO — GMA designations are regional water-resource extraction/recharge management regimes rather than last-mile service-access rules, and SDWA primacy (Tribal vs State) and CWS vs DWA status are broad jurisdictional/compliance categories analyzed in relation to aquifer water-table trends and contaminant mobilization rather than rule-type mechanisms directly governing household service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure rules, tariffs, disconnections, or utility access regulation).
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Quantitative spatial ecological empirical study across 1,881 drinking water service areas in Arizona combining ADWR index well water-level records (2001–2020), 27,334 arsenic and 47,783 nitrate observations (1998–2019), and 2020 U.S. Census data using Moran's I, Getis-Ord Gi*, ANOVA, and multivariate regressions.
criterion_notes.c4: No. All empirical outcomes reported are either (1) hydrogeological subbasin groundwater-table level changes/declines in ft/year from ADWR index wells over 10- and 20-year periods (water-resource stock/depletion) or (2) groundwater nitrate and arsenic concentrations, detections, and MCL exceedances (water quality/contamination). No outcome measures household or community service access, connection, tap service availability, continuity/reliability, delivered water quantity, affordability, or disconnection/exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. The unit of analysis (1,881 drinking water service areas in Arizona), explanatory variables, hydrogeological and water-quality outcomes, and spatial ecological regression/clustering study design are clearly identified.

study_design: Spatial ecological observational study using geostatistical clustering (Moran's I, Getis-Ord Gi*, k-means/hierarchical clustering), ANOVA, and multivariate linear and logistic regression over 10- and 20-year periods
population_and_sample: 1,881 groundwater-supplied drinking water service areas in Arizona (55.3% regulated community water systems [CWS] and 44.7% unregulated private domestic well areas [DWAs]), integrating 27,334 arsenic and 47,783 nitrate observations (1998–2019), ADWR index well groundwater-level data (2001–2020), and 2020 U.S. Census demographic/housing data
exposure: Regulatory and governance classifications (Arizona 1980 Groundwater Management Act designation: Non-Designated Areas vs Active Management Areas/Irrigation Non-Expansion Areas; Safe Drinking Water Act primacy: Tribal vs State oversight; supply type: Domestic Well Areas vs Community Water Systems), aquifer type (karst vs alluvial), and Census service-area demographic and housing characteristics
outcome: Subbasin groundwater-table level change/decline rates over 20-year (2001–2020) and 10-year (2011–2020) periods (ft/year and binary decline indicator from ADWR index wells), and groundwater arsenic and nitrate concentrations, detections, and regulatory Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) exceedances
rationale: Exclude (E04: Wrong outcome). Although this empirical spatial ecological study of 1,881 Arizona drinking water service areas uses the term 'access' in its conceptual framework and includes regulatory classifications (Groundwater Management Act designations, Tribal vs State SDWA primacy, and CWS vs exempt DWA supply types) as predictors, 'access' in the paper refers only to those static predictor attributes. Its actual measured outcomes are (1) hydrogeological subbasin aquifer water-table level changes/declines (ft/year from ADWR index wells) and (2) groundwater arsenic and nitrate concentrations, detections, and MCL exceedances (water quality). It does not report any household or community water service access outcome (such as connection, tap service availability, continuity/reliability, delivered water quantity, affordability, or disconnection/exclusion), nor does it evaluate a last-mile rule-type mechanism governing service access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification.
